summaries.summary: NER is crucial for information extraction and higher-level tasks, with recall critical because ungenerated candidates cannot be recovered later.
NER is formulated as sequential word labeling with BIO2 labels for non-recursive, non-overlapping mentions, using recurrent neural networks for contextual token prediction.
Common recall-loss errors include misspellings, POS errors, capitalization, unseen words and irregular context, motivating three generalization layers.
Dictionary-based vectors suffer from sparse training sets, with 27% unseen words in GENIA for pretrained word2vec, motivating letter-trigram word hashing.
Word shape properties are important for NER, so words use lowercase letter-trigrams plus flag bits for capitalization and case surface information.
Sparse idiosyncratic data requires strong generalization, and LSTMs are applied to sequence labeling for long-range context-sensitive information and high 80–90% NER F1 performance.
The model feeds letter-trigram vectors into a bidirectional LSTM and combines both directions in a second LSTM layer for label prediction.
Word encodings and labels are real-valued vectors, and the LSTM uses gates, internal state, duplicated bidirectional states, and BPTT training.
The network iterates over labeled sentences in mini-batches, updates weights, and predicts label probabilities for unseen word sequences.
The bidirectional LSTM model is evaluated on three neural network configurations implemented with Deeplearning4j and Stanford CoreNLP preprocessing.
The paragraph contains only the marker [noitemsep].
DICT builds a dictionary over all corpus words and generates input vectors using 1-hot encoding for each word.
EMB uses GoogleNews word2vec embeddings, encoding each word as a vector of size 300.
TRI implements letter-trigram word hashing as described in Section SECREF14.
During training and test, sentence tokens are grouped as mini-batch, and three neural network types evaluate the bidirectional sequence learner.
FF is a feed-forward baseline with 3 hidden layers of size 150, relu activation, a 3-class softmax classifier, and learning rate of 0.005.
LSTM uses a feed-forward layer of size 150, two single-direction LSTM layers with 20 cells, a 3-class softmax classifier, BPTT, and learning rate of 0.005.
BLSTM uses a feed-forward layer of size 150, one bidirectional LSTM layer with 20 cells, an additional single-direction LSTM with 20 cells, and a 3-class softmax classifier.
Nine configurations are evaluated on five gold standard data sets, with letter-trigram word hashing and bidirectional LSTM yielding the best results.
Two identically parameterized models use 2000 randomly chosen labeled sentences, and TRI+BLSTM training takes approximately 50 minutes on a commodity Intel i7 notebook with 4 cores at 2.8GHz.
Training data sets include GENIA Corpus with GENIA technical term annotations 3.02 and CoNLL2003 based on the Reuters RCV-1 news corpus.
Testing uses CoNLL2003-testA, a 50 document split from GENIA, and complete KORE50, ACE2004 and MSNBC data sets using GERBIL.
DATEXIS-NER and state-of-the-art annotators are measured with precision, recall and F1 score, weak annotation match, and token-level BIO2 labeling performance.
Overall mention annotation performance uses measures from cornolti2013framework and ling2015design, comparing gold standard mention annotations with predicted annotations.
The comparison uses a weak annotation match.
The measurement uses micro-averaged precision, recall and NER-style score.
For model tuning, label classes are measured separately with binary classification precision, recall and scores, using macro-averaging over the three classes.
The evaluation discusses DATEXIS-NER on common and idiosyncratic data.
DATEXIS-NER achieves highest recall of 95%–98%, equal or better than median precision, and micro-F1 scores of 84%–94% on news entity recognition.
On biomedical entity recognition, DATEXIS-NER outperforms HMM, MEMM, CRF and CDN based models with micro-F1 score of 84%, while the GENIA chunker for LingPipe scores higher.
On CoNLL2003 and GENIA, letter-trigram word vectors with bidirectional LSTM report highest macro-F1 scores for BIO2 labeling, while DICT, EMB and TRI show different strengths.
The contextual LSTM model achieves scores in the 85%–94% range, outperforms the FF baseline maximum of 75%, and bidirectional LSTMs improve precision and recall.
DATEXIS-NER components are investigated by manual inspection of classification errors for false negative detections, false positives and invalid boundaries.
Dictionary misses cause false negatives in DICT and word2vec, while the letter-trigram approach resolves this error despite possible unseen trigrams such as thh.
Case-sensitive word vectorization causes false positives from incorrect capitalization, so lowercase word vectors with surface form feature flags achieve best results.
Ambiguous co-occurring mention groups encode strong syntagmatic word relations, so correct boundaries require contextual models such as LSTMs.
Paradigmatic relation groups are efficiently represented in word2vec, but letter-trigram vectors require a larger training sample to capture these relations.
Some synonyms require larger document context than local sentence context, affecting named entity disambiguation and coreference resolution more than NER recall.
DATEXIS-NER recognizes boundaries of generic mentions without NER-style typing, with specific types possible via multiple independent models and a longest-span semantic type heuristic.
NER depends on specific problem context, while most approaches use fixed datasets in batch mode and often suffer from poor recall.
The work reports F1 scores between 84–94% using bidirectional multi-layered LSTMs, letter-trigram word hashing and surface form features on only few hundred training examples.

Future work will target health, life science, fashion, engineering or automotive domains, joint mention detection and ontology linking, and interactive workflows for personalized named entity linking systems.
